This study helps to provide an understanding of the Syrian Orthodox Church in the more recent past. In particular, it seeks to relate how that Church experienced contact with the Church of England. data.title: An Analysis of the Syriac Text of the Book of Daniel
data.abstractNote: This investigation of the Syriac text of the Book of Daniel seeks primarily to address two issues. First, it defines the textual affinities of this version in terms of its relationship to the MT and its relationship to the other ancient versions of the Old Testament. Such an understanding of the textual affinities of the Syriac version is essential to establishing its proper role in the text-critical process. Second, it describes the translation characteristics and techniques of this version so as to evaluate its adequacy as a translation. Awareness of the translation techniques will also inform the text-critical use of this version. This study first isolates the textual and translational features of the Syriac version of the Book of Daniel which set if off from the Hebrew/Aramaic text of the MT and then considers those distinctive features in the light of evidence from the LXX, Theodotion-Daniel, the Sahidic Coptic, and the Latin Vulgate. It is demonstrated that the text before the Syriac translator was remarkably close to the MT; however, the version also exhibits influence from certain other sources. There is, for example, occasional agreement with the LXX, and there is considerable affinity with Theodotion-Daniel. The conclusion is drawn that while the Syriac version of the Book of Daniel was translated from a Hebrew/Aramaic text, it was also significantly influenced by Theodotion-Daniel. Its value as a textual witness is most significant therefore when it differs both from MT and from Theodotion-Daniel. In a limited number of instances the Syriac version alone has preserved the superior text. As a translation the Syriac version of the Book of Daniel is an accurate and faithful rendering of its Vorlage, while at the same time commending itself as a very readable and idiomatic translation. At times, however, it is pleonastic and expansionistic, and it occasionally shows a tendency to reverse the order of pairs of words. The translation was probably made in the second century A.D. At present it is not possible to say for sure whether it originated in a Jewish or in a Christian community.

data.abstractNote: The church of Gola is one of the few religious buildings with bema located outside the diocese of Antioch. Dated from the end of the 5th or the 6th century ce, it is located in a valley between the Mesopotamian plain and the Upper Tigris. Its architectural features and mosaic pavement testify to the influence of northern Syria, especially the regions of Apamea and Antioch. The main carpet represents the toil of the spring months along with a scene of hunting and animals chasing each other. The mosaic features several Syriac inscriptions, including a dedication that states the date on which the paving was made. The position of the building, at the edge of the Eastern Roman Empire, prompts us to explore the cultural relations of this region with other parts of the empire and to examine its local context, in the cradle of the Syriac world.
